newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, Romania initial friendship treaty.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, Romania initial friendship treaty.

text.p: The foreign ministers of Ukraine and Romania initialled on Saturday a long-delayed post-Communist friendship treaty that may improve Bucharest's chances for early NATO membership.

Hennady Udovenko of Ukraine told a news conference the document proclaimed the present borders between the two countries "inviolable" and said neither nation would have any claims on the territory of the other.
Udovenko and Adrian Severin of Romania initialled the treaty, which is due to be formally signed by the presidents of the two countries and ratified by their parliaments.

The Soviet Union seized chunks of Romanian territory in 1940 under the secret Soviet-German pact and these territories, including northern Bukovina and southern Bessarabia, became part of Ukraine after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

"There is an article in the document confirming the inviolability of the existing borders and proclaiming that (both sides) would not have any territorial claims to each other now and in the future," Udovenko said.
"This treaty aims at strenthening Ukraine's territorial integrity. This is the factor of stability in our region," Severin said. "Noone has lost."

Sources in the Ukrainian foreign ministry told Reuters that the treaty, a subject of tense debated for three years, is expected to be signed by Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma and Romanian President Emil Constantinescu later this month.
Both sides, the sources said, wanted the treaty to be ratified before NATO summit in Madrid in July.
Severin, whose country seeks membership in the Western alliance, has denied that Bucharest wanted to use the treaty with Ukraine as a "bargaining chip".
Romania won praise from the West for signing a treaty with Hungary last year ending old rifts over borders and minorities with its Western neighbour.
Some Western leaders have said a similar deal with Kiev could improve Romania's chances for early NATO membership.
The Western alliance is expected to issue the first invitations to Eastern European countries in Madrid. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are believed to be the favourites.

Ukraine and Romania still have differences in drawing the naval border in the Black Sea, which both sides believe is rich in natural gas and oil. These differences are due to be resolved at another treaty to be completed in the next two years.

The foreign ministry sources said the two sides will turn to the International Court of Justice in the Hague if they fail to come to terms on the demarcation of the sea shelf -- particularly near the Serpent island.
Until then, they have promised a moratorium on geological works at the shelf. Experts say that some 7,000 square km (4,000 square miles) of sea are disputed.
